title: Sindhi devotees of Nanak
hookLine: many Sindhi families revere Guru Nanak and the Granth

cards: Before breakfast, a grandmother in a Sindhi family's home covers her head and steps into a small room kept a little differently from the rest of the house. The floor is swept twice.

A cloth canopy hangs over a low platform, and on it, wrapped in fine cloth, rests a copy of the Guru Granth Sahib. A picture of Guru Nanak hangs nearby. On the same shelf there might be images from a Hindu shrine too.
She reads a few lines of the Japji, then goes to make the tea. Nobody in the house wears a turban. Today we meet a devotion to Guru Nanak that has its own shape.

teach.b: Nanakpanthi means one who walks on Nanak's path. It's a name used for people who revere Guru Nanak and the Granth whether or not they keep the Khalsa's outward form. In some Sindhi Hindu families the devotion runs deep.
Tradition in Sindh remembers Guru Nanak's teaching reaching there through traveling teachers, and some Sindhi families came to hold the Granth as sacred and Guru Nanak as their own.
Sindhi devotees gather at places called darbars or tikanas, where the Granth is honored and kirtan is sung, often beside images and customs from Hindu worship.
A Sindhi family might name a child at the Granth, or read Sukhmani Sahib at a death. The Partition carried Sindhi families far from Sindh, and tradition remembers some carrying the Granth with them.

Sikhs see this devotion in different ways. Some welcome it warmly as love for the Guru. Others are concerned about the Granth being placed beside images, since Sikh practice keeps the Guru Granth Sahib apart.
Those conversations are real, sometimes hard, and they belong to the people having them. Underneath both is a line Guru Nanak sang, kept in the Sohila on Ang 13.
In paraphrase: there is a light in everyone, and that light is the One; by its shining, all are lit.
Nanak's word didn't stop at the edge of one community. It traveled to Sindh, into homes that keep it in their own way.

how: Some Sindhi families keep the Guru Granth Sahib in their homes or gather at darbars and tikanas to hear it read and sung, honoring Guru Nanak as their own, often alongside Hindu customs.

games.q: a Sindhi friend invites you to a reading of Sukhmani Sahib at their family darbar. there are images from a Hindu shrine nearby. what does this lesson ask of you?
o: point out what they're doing wrong.
see the love in it, and let it be theirs.
decline, since it isn't your way.
games.why: today's practice: honor a devotion unlike yours. Sikhs discuss the questions; the love is plain to see.

practice: Call to mind someone who loves something holy in a way you don't, a different ritual, a mix you wouldn't choose, and don't decide whether they're right.
Just see the love in it, the swept floor, the covered head, the few lines before breakfast; breathe in that love, and breathe out, letting it be theirs.

wordCard.voice: Nanakpanthi. One who walks on Nanak's path. A name for people, among them Sindhi families, who revere Guru Nanak and the Granth in their own way. Today's word.
